52716-the-business-of-being-a-housewife-:
Jean Prescott Adams wrote a guide to run a home as a sound trade. A second form came out in Chicago in 1921. Adams led food thrift work for Armour and Company. Meat is a chief cost in the American diet, the book starts. Live beasts and cut meat can not be set side by side, it warns.

A live beast is not all meat, and a carcass not all steaks. Fair math must guide the wife who weighs the shops' claims. Cuts, waste, and the mid man's share each take their due. Plans for buys, stores, and meals fill the book's core. Home keepers get a meat firm's own brief in full. Each page aims at thrift.
69052-the-ward-of-tecumseh:
Crittenden Marriott wrote The Ward of Tecumseh, for Lippincott in 1914. Philadelphia and London shared the edition of the romance. McKernan drew its illustrations, with a council fire as front plate. Alagwa comes to the council fire in that frontispiece scene. Sally Castleton, Southerner was Marriott's earlier tale, the ads note.

Alagwa, being wounded, is rescued by Jack Telfair in one plate. Alagwa shoots Captain Brito in another of the listed pictures. Jack Telfair and Captain Brito settle their dispute in a third. Chapter one opens as Sally Habersham accepts Dick Ogilvie. Her mother's friends did not exactly rejoice at the match, it owns. Sundry masculine satellites return to their orbits at the news, it jokes. The ward herself stands between two worlds in the tale's frame. Marriott gives Tecumseh's time a romance of the border.
britannica-1911-abadeh: Abadeh is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry sets the small walled town in Persia's province of Fars, on a fertile plain at 6,200 feet. It stands on the high road between Isfahan and Shiraz, nearer the first than the second. Four thousand people are counted there. The town chiefs a district of thirty villages and holds post and telegraph offices. Its fame rests on carved wood-work: small boxes, trays, and sherbet spoons cut from pear and box wood, the entry reports.
britannica-1911-cutler-manasseh:
Manasseh Cutler, an American clergyman who lived from 1742 to 1823, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Killingly in Connecticut, he left Yale in 1765. He taught school, traded, and at times pled in court before he chose the ministry. From 1771 till his death he was pastor at what is now Hamilton in Massachusetts.

In the War of Independence he served as a chaplain. He trained in medicine to add to a thin income and ran a boarding school for some 25 years. As agent of the Ohio Company he won a contract with Congress for 1,500,000 acres north of the Ohio. He also had a lead hand in drafting the Ordinance of 1787. He sat in Congress from 1801 to 1805, and his range ran to botany and the stars as well.
britannica-1911-leh:
Leh is the capital of Ladakh in India, set high above the upper Indus river. It stands eleven thousand five hundred feet above the sea, the entry says. Roads from Srinagar and from Yarkand both reach the town over long miles. Leh is the great market for trade between India, Chinese Turkestan, and Tibet. Routes from Kashgar, Yarkand, Khotan, and Lhasa all meet there.

Two chief roads link Leh with India, by Srinagar and by the Kulu valley. A British officer is sent to Leh under a trade treaty with Kashmir. He helps control the traders and traffic with the state's governor. Leh has long been the start point for bold trips into Tibet. A Moravian mission stands there with a small hospital. Its weather station is the highest in Asia, and rain is very scant.
britannica-1911-panjdeh:
Panjdeh, a village of Russian Turkestan, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It was made famous by the Panjdeh scare of 1885. The village stands on the east side of the Kushk river, near its junction with the Murghab. In March 1885 a boundary commission was meant to settle the Russo-Afghan line. This portion of the line was in dispute between Afghans and Russians.

An Afghan force camped on the west bank of the Kushk. On March 29 General Komarov sent an ultimatum demanding their withdrawal. On their refusal, the Russians attacked before dawn on March 30. They drove the Afghans across the bridge with a loss of some 600 men. The clash nearly brought war between England and Russia. The amir treated it as a mere frontier scuffle. The line later drawn gave Russia the corner between the two rivers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gezireh:
Gezireh, also called Djezireh, held two Catholic residential sees, one Chaldean and one Syrian, on the right bank of the Tigris. The Chaldean diocese traced its line back to Beit-Zabdai, known since 410. The Syrian see grew from Jacobite bishops who entered Catholic communion. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sets out both dioceses as they stood in the early twentieth century.

The Chaldean diocese then counted four thousand faithful and fourteen priests. It held seventeen churches and chapels, with a dozen schools for boys and one for girls. The smaller Syrian diocese counted five hundred faithful, eleven priests, five churches, and six schools. The town itself, Gezireh-ibn-Omar, held about ten thousand people, six thousand of them Catholics. Watered soil, oak forests, and a rich oil well some twenty-five miles away shaped its setting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isaac-of-nine:
A seventh-century Nestorian bishop of Nineveh, Isaac was first a monk at Bethabe in Kurdistan, consecrated by Patriarch George, who ruled from 660 to 680. After only five months as bishop he stepped down for unknown reasons and retired to the monastery of Rabban Shapur, where he died old and blind from study and austerity. Late in life his Nestorian orthodoxy came under suspicion.

Three theses of his won little favor among Nestorians, and Daniel Bar Tubanita, bishop of Beth Garmai, became his ardent opponent. Their exact contents are lost, but they ran too Catholic for Nestorian teaching. A surviving prayer to Christ, the entry notes, reads so Catholic that claiming so great a writer has tempted both sides. Readers meet a monk-bishop whose writings outlived his church's doubts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jehovah-yahwe:
Jehovah, also rendered Yahweh, is God's own name in the Old Testament, called by Jews the name above all names, the great, glorious, and hidden name. Most often it is shem hammephorash, the explicit or separated name. Concordances count it about six thousand times, alone or joined to another divine name, more than any other.

Greek and Latin Bibles generally render it Lord, translating Adonai, the word readers spoke in its place. Fathers and rabbis alike treat it as ineffable, beyond utterance, and modern Jews remain unsure of its true sound. The entry traces its forms, its reverent substitutes, and the long debate over how a name too holy to speak should be read.
doe-osti-3378000-comparison-of-radiosond:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-23228, printed July 2026, compares two radiosonde datasets: SondeHub and the Integrated Global Radiosonde Archive. The authors are Minjae Cho, Sarah Albert, and Elizabeth Silber, all of Sandia in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Radiosondes are the weather instruments carried aloft by balloons, and their records feed forecasts and climate work.

The comparison proceeds on set axes. First, data availability within the United States, then global availability, then data quality, then the number of frames each archive holds. A final section treats radiosonde ascent and descent, the two halves of a flight that archives may record unevenly. Conclusions close the short report. For a user choosing between a community-fed archive and the official one, the side-by-side counts are the practical value.
